en: Land heats faster than the ocean during the day, causing warm air to rise and cooler ocean air to rush inland as a sea breeze.
The Moon's gravitational pull creates a bulge in Earth's oceans, causing water levels to rise and fall as the planet rotates through the bulges.
Extreme pressure and temperature in a star's core force hydrogen atoms to fuse into helium, releasing the massive light and heat energy we see.
Intense underground heat and pressure squeeze and recrystallize existing limestone minerals, transforming the sedimentary rock into hard, non-foliated metamorphic marble.
Friction locks tectonic plates together until built-up stress suddenly overcomes the friction, releasing energy as seismic waves that shake the ground during an earthquake.
Plant roots absorb groundwater and release it as water vapor through leaf pores, adding moisture to the atmosphere to help form rain clouds.
Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to receive varying angles of direct sunlight throughout the year, creating the four seasons.
Rainwater mixes with carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which chemically weathers and dissolves limestone bedrock to carve out large underground caves.
Earthworms consume decaying organic matter and excrete nutrient-rich castings, which improves soil fertility and creates tunnels that allow air and water to reach plant roots.
Subducting oceanic crust melts into magma that rises through cracks in the continental plate, building pressure until it erupts explosively as a volcano.
Warm tropical ocean water evaporates and rises rapidly, releasing latent heat that fuels the strong, rotating winds and heavy rainfall of a typhoon.
The Moon orbits directly between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight and casting a dark shadow on Earth's surface to create a solar eclipse.
